title: Coval vs Hamming in 2026: The Voice Agent Testing Platform Built for Regulated Industries
summary: Coval vs Hamming compared for regulated industries: human review, backend checks, public docs, and pricing, with a clear verdict. See the comparison.
body_markdown:
If you’re choosing a voice agent testing platform for a bank, a clinic, or an insurer, it has to answer two questions: can you trust its scores, and did the agent really do what it told the caller? Coval vs Hamming comes down to how each platform answers them, and Coval is the better choice. It’s the more mature company, with a[$28 million Series A](https://www.coval.ai/blog/coval-series-a/) and a[founder](https://www.coval.ai/about-us/) who led evaluation infrastructure at Waymo, and it’s built for regulated industries like yours.


Human review is at the core of how Coval answers the first question, whether you can trust the scores. Both platforms score calls with an AI judge, a language model that grades each conversation. Hamming’s pitch highlights how accurate its judge is, while Coval sends the calls its judge flags to your own reviewers and measures the judge against their answers. For the second, Coval goes to your backend: after each test call, it reads the record the agent should have changed, say a card’s status, and checks it against the value you expect.


Both also simulate voice and chat agents, monitor production calls, turn failed ones into[regression tests](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/uploaded-conversations/overview) , and cover SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA. So the six criteria below focus on where they differ, starting with who each platform is built for and ending with what it costs to start.

*The two questions a regulated team needs answered, and how Coval answers each one.*


## Track record: Coval is built for regulated industries, and Zoom and Chime test with it


In[financial services](https://www.coval.ai/industries/financial-services/) ,[healthcare](https://www.coval.ai/industries/healthcare/) , and[insurance](https://www.coval.ai/industries/insurance/) , one wrong answer from a voice agent can become a regulatory problem, and those are the industries Coval is built for. Its approach comes from Waymo, where[each code change](https://www.coval.ai/blog/coval-raises-3-3-to-to-bring-self-driving-car-simulation-to-ai-voice-chat-agents/) was tested in a virtual environment before deployment, and Coval applies the same discipline to voice and chat agents. The customers are there too. In financial services, Chime tests its voice agents with Coval, and Zoom, Deepgram, and Fortune 500 enterprises are among the[more than 60 organizations](https://www.coval.ai/blog/new-self-improving-agents/) that use it. Zoom’s QA team runs daily scheduled regression tests on Coval, and across all its customers, Coval runs[3.1M evaluation metrics](https://www.coval.ai/) a week. Security review won’t separate the two platforms. SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA come on every Coval plan, Enterprise adds SAML SSO and SCIM, and single-tenant deployments are available. Hamming also offers[SSO and single-tenant deployment](https://hamming.ai/enterprise) . What separates them is focus. Hamming serves a broad mix of industries and is less focused on regulated teams than Coval. Coval’s focus on those teams shapes the two checks we care about most: whether the judge agrees with your reviewers, and whether the agent really changed your system or only said it did.


## Human review: Coval proves its AI judge against your own reviewers


When a failed test blocks a release, someone will ask whether your human reviewers would have failed that call. A QA or compliance lead needs that answer before trusting any score, so Coval keeps people in the loop instead of trusting the judge alone. It gets the answer from your own calls with a[review project](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/human-review/human-review) , which groups the conversations to review, the metrics to label, and the people assigned.


Your reviewers don’t have to be engineers. QA and compliance staff give their own answer for each metric in a[no-code interface](https://www.coval.ai/products/human-review/) , and they don’t wade through a random sample, either. Auto-add rules pull in new conversations whose metric results match conditions you set, such as every call where the AI-disclosure metric failed, and Coval sends the calls where the judge is uncertain or the behavior looks off to the top of your review queue. Shared rubrics and inter-rater agreement tracking keep reviewers consistent with each other, so their answers are a baseline worth measuring the judge against.


Agreement between the judge and your reviewers can hide a useless metric. Our[docs](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/human-review/insights) show why: when reviewers mark 95 of 100 conversations as successful, a metric that marks all 100 successful has 95% agreement but catches none of the five failures. So for each binary metric, Coval reports three numbers on your reviewed calls: agreement, catch rate, and κ. Catch rate is the share of human-flagged problems the metric also flagged, and κ is agreement corrected for chance. Hamming supports call review, annotations, and custom score review, but its pitch highlights the accuracy of its AI judge. Coval starts from the other end: the judge has to prove itself against your reviewers.


When a metric’s numbers look wrong, the error-direction view shows whether it misses real problems or raises false alarms. After you change the metric, rerun it on the calls your reviewers already labeled to see whether the fix worked before it goes back into a release check.


In one[published case](https://www.coval.ai/blog/how-to-create-ai-judge-metrics-you-can-trust/) , a team running an outbound voice agent checked whether the agent disclosed that it’s an AI. Its disclosure metric agreed with reviewers on 89% of 314 conversations, a number that looks healthy but doesn’t say which way the 35 disagreements went. The error-direction view sorts them into failures the judge missed and false alarms, and for a compliance check, the misses are exactly the failures you’re paying the judge to find.


## Backend outcomes: Coval checks what the call changed in your system


A judge you trust still only grades what it hears. The other question after a failed test is whether the agent did what it told the caller, and that is a question for your backend. After the simulated call, Coval’s[API State metric](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/types/deterministic) calls your API, reads the field you name, and compares it with the value you expect. It returns MATCH, DIFF, or NOT_FOUND with no LLM involved, so the same response always gets the same result.


Take a lost-card flow. First, a[pre-simulation API call](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/test-sets/api-simulation-wrappers) (beta) sets up a test cardholder with an active card. The simulated caller reports the card lost, and after the call the API State metric fetches the card’s status and expects FROZEN. An agent that tells the caller “your card is frozen” without ever freezing it sounds right in the transcript and still gets DIFF.


Chime runs the same kind of test. It creates a user through the API before a simulation, and after the call it makes a follow-up API call to check card status, account freezes, and other state changes the agent was supposed to produce.


Hamming also scores business outcomes and tool-call evidence. What sets Coval’s check apart is that it’s publicly documented, so you can see exactly how it decides a pass before you buy.


## Simulation: Coval tests with real-world audio, its own judge, and 1,000 concurrent calls


The judge and the backend check are only as good as the test calls behind them, and a regulated team needs calls that sound like its real ones. Each of Coval’s simulated callers carries a[persona](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/personas/overview) , which sets the caller’s voice, accent, and speaking style. Coval simulates the caller’s voice and the background sound together, something competitors can’t do, so the agent hears a caller on a noisy line just as it would in production. You can pick from a built-in library of sounds or upload your own. And when you need to see how an agent holds up under production-scale traffic, Coval’s[load testing](https://docs.coval.ai/changelog) runs 1,000 concurrent simulated calls, no questions asked, which competitors don’t offer. You don’t have to pick a judge model for those calls. By default, the AI judge runs on the Coval Judge, our own fine-tuned model paired with a custom judging algorithm, and the review project from earlier tells you how often it agrees with your reviewers.


## Release workflow: Coval runs from your terminal, coding agent, and CI


All of this only helps if it runs on every change, before the release ships. Coval is[CLI and API first](https://www.coval.ai/products/simulation/) , so the checks run where your team already works. Engineers script runs from the terminal or with typed[TypeScript and Python SDKs](https://docs.coval.ai/sdks/overview) . Coding agents can launch them too: the[MCP connector](https://docs.coval.ai/mcp/overview) works from ChatGPT, Claude, and Codex, and Coval’s[agent skills](https://docs.coval.ai/agents/skills) run in Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, and 40+ other coding agents. In CI, the[GitHub Action](https://github.com/coval-ai/coval-github-action) fails the job when any simulation returns the metric value you mark as a failure. With[mutations](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/agents/mutations) , which are versions of your agent with a different prompt or model, you can run the same test set against each one and see exactly what changed.


Our docs are public, too, with an[llms.txt index](https://docs.coval.ai/llms.txt) your coding agent can read.


Hamming offers REST, SDKs, webhooks, an MCP server, and CI quality gates. Its[documentation](https://docs.hamming.ai/) asks for an access code before you can read it.


## Coval vs Hamming pricing: Coval publishes its plans and offers a free trial


That leaves cost, and what it takes to find all this out for yourself. As of October 2026, Coval’s[Starter plan](https://www.coval.ai/pricing/) costs $100 a month, Growth $500 a month, and Enterprise starts at $4,500 a month. Starter and Growth begin with a 7-day free trial. Every plan includes simulation, monitoring, and human review, with unlimited seats. Starter covers 100 simulation minutes a month, then $0.40 per extra minute.


Hamming lists “Contact us” on[all three of its plans](https://hamming.ai/pricing) and prices mainly by test volume. Its[FAQ](https://hamming.ai/faqs) says: “We don’t offer a traditional free trial with self-serve access.”


Getting to a first test is fast. The[Coval CLI](https://docs.coval.ai/welcome) takes you from install to your first simulation in under 15 minutes. You can[build a test set](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/test-sets/create) by hand, draft one with the Coval Test Set Generator, or upload the cases you already have from a CSV or XLSX file. From there, teams move quickly:[Krew](https://www.coval.ai/blog/how-krew-runs-10-000-voice-ai-evaluations-monthly-with-coval-(and-turns-qa-into-sales-acceleration)/) , which runs 10,000+ voice AI evaluations a month on Coval, made it core infrastructure for its engineering team within two months.


And you don’t have to do the setup yourself. Enterprise teams get white-glove onboarding with a named engineer, and you can send us your agent’s phone number for a[free audit](https://www.coval.ai/voice-agent-audit/) : we run 30+ simulations against every behavior you select and report back in two business days.

The next time that call blocks a release, you’ll have the catch rate and the backend record to show your compliance team why.
